II. From "From this" onwards, the introduction is set forth; it is also called the specific introduction. This section has two parts: first, listing the two names.
Although these are alternative names, they also possess distinctions of length. Describing the "Preface Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*), it separately exhausts the first division.
Because this preface differs from those of other sutras, it is given a distinct name; it is called the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, thus we know that this preface is the basis for these alternative names.

First, regarding "entering meditative concentration": the Great Awakened One’s sudden, perfect illumination is eternally quiescent.
His present entry into concentration is intended to demonstrate the ritual procedure so that people may delight in meditative absorption.
Second, regarding "narration": having entered this wondrous concentration and perceived the noble majesty of the Dharma, he then narrates this King of Sutras within this very state of concentration.

Regarding the statement "emerging from [samādhi]," it does not actually indicate the physical manifestation of emerging from concentration; rather, because quiescence does not obstruct illumination, one speaks of "emerging.
The Buddha did not actually emerge from concentration when he preached this sutra; his intention was fundamentally to demonstrate that within quiescence there is illumination.

Next, regarding the "doubter": since it has been stated that the Dharma is what the Buddha realized, the one with the mark of faith (Śraddhālakṣaṇa) then wonders why the lifespan of the person who realized it is not commensurate with the Dharma.
The sequence in the *Ruiying* (Sutra of Auspicious Responses) and other texts is clear and can be understood from the text itself.
2. From "Or at times" onwards, the three distinctions are clarified.
The Great Master occasionally made these distinctions, which were recorded by Zhàngān; they differ from the previous seven only in their manner of opening and closing.
Second, from "The Narrative" (*yan xu*) onwards, the description of the characteristics has two parts:
first, the actual presentation of the narrative.

Regarding the description of those harboring doubts: they contemplate the profound meaning [of the Dharma], yet necessarily harbor doubt that the Dharma realized must be eternal while the life-span of the realizer is short.
Regarding the introduction on severing doubts: Buddhapālita’s primary aim was to sever doubts and engender faith.
Regarding the introduction to the "Chapter on Repentance": its direct purpose is to destroy evil, while its secondary purpose is to give rise to goodness.
The introduction to the "Chapter on Praise" is primarily intended to engender wholesome qualities and secondarily to eliminate unwholesome ones.

The introduction to the "Chapter on Emptiness" is intended to lead toward the accomplishment of engendering wholesome qualities and extinguishing unwholesome ones; the present text specifically introduces it because it extinguishes the three obstacles.
Mahābrahmā and Śakra are the lords of Vaiśravaṇa (Saṃjñeya).
The kiṃnaras and others are the followers and subordinates led by Vaiśravaṇa.
The sūtra cites the leaders to describe their respective classes.

Regarding the introduction to the "Orthodox Discourse" (Zhenglun) and the "Excellent Collection" (Shanji): the "Orthodox Discourse" concerns the cultivation of the garden, while the "Excellent Collection" concerns listening to the sutras; as both are outflows from the secret treasury, they are introduced here under the heading of "Secret."
Regarding the introduction to the "Prediction" (vyākaraṇa): because his mind became as pure as space upon hearing the sutra, he received the prediction.
It is now stated that this is because his body and mind are free from defilement.

Regarding the introduction to the "Chapter on Relinquishing the Body": since the Prince’s body was consumed and he attained liberation, this demonstrates that his life was sustained not by improper food; therefore, the single phrase "right livelihood" is now used to introduce it.

Regarding the introduction to the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha": although there are three sections in which bodhisattvas praise the Buddha in verse, these bodhisattvas are for the most part ancient buddhas; even those who are currently practicing as realizations are likewise future buddhas. Therefore, the practitioners whom the present Buddha praises are also future buddhas; hence, this chapter is introduced.
"Seemingly" (*fǎngfēi*) refers to an appearance that is not distinct.
*Wěi* (薳) is pronounced *wěi*, meaning "distant.
It is as if one cannot exceed the boundaries of what is clearly manifest for oneself.

First, an explanation based on the meaning.

In the *Fahua wenju*, each of the three bodies has both the meaning of "suchness" (*tathatā*) and the meaning of "coming. Here, "suchness" is explained by the mutual merging of the Dharma-body and the Reward-body, while "coming" is explained by the appearance of the Response-body in the world; however, as long as the meaning is established, it matters not whether the interpretation is general or specific.
If the Buddha follows wisdom, he should be like the secret treasury; yet it is solely for the sake of following compassion that he comes into the triple world.

the "capable vehicle" is wisdom, the "path according to reality" is principle, and "coming to achieve" refers to the manifestation of compassionate response.
Second, from "Great" (*dai*) onwards, the explanation is given in terms of wisdom and practice.

Although it simply says "comes," it already encompasses the meaning of "Tathāgata" (*nyorai*); for when one comes with merit and wisdom to adorn the Dharma-body, that which is adorned is precisely the Tathāgata.
This is the explanation of the name "Tathāgata" from the "Brahmacarya Chapter" of the *Mahāsūtra*.

The dharmas that have existed from the beginning constitute their characteristics within the wondrous True, the Conventional, and the Middle.
When wisdom accords with this understanding, the Dharma-body and the Reward-body merge; therefore, it is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
To call this "as it is spoken" means that the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) adapts to the capacities of sentient beings; thus, it is called "coming.
Previously, the discussion was based on compassion and wisdom, and its meaning remained general.
Now, by clarifying the explanation of the characteristics of the three truths (tridharmalakṣaṇa), the term "Tathāgata" is interpreted so that no aspect of its meaning is left unexhausted.
The characteristics of the three truths are the three *dharmakāyas*; their perfection is the *dharmakāya*.
To understand them in accordance with this is the three *prajñās*; their perfection is the *saṃbhogakāya*.
To explain them in accordance with this is the three liberations; their perfection is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Viewed from the present in light of the past, there is indeed a distinction.
Third, the section beginning with "The one who wanders" explains the character "to wander.
This refers to the Tathāgata’s entry into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) by means of ultimate wisdom.

Regarding the Dharma-nature that is realized and the resultant wisdom that realizes it, although they are established conceptually as "subject" and "object," their essence does not involve mutual contact.
Because ultimate initial awakening is identical to original awakening, only the wisdom of True Suchness remains.
Therefore, if this is so, who is able to enter?
And what is there to enter?
It is the same for abiding and emerging.
The intent of the citation from the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* is likewise the same.
What is now called "wandering" is a manifestation of entering [the truth] shown for the purpose of leading sentient beings to study the Buddha-dharma and enter into principle.
In order to cause sentient beings to abide in accordance with the principle, he manifests the characteristic of abiding.
Ambrosia (*amṛta*) is the medicine of immortality; it is a metaphor for the eternal principle.
To speak this flavor of ambrosia for the sake of sentient beings, one should also say that it "issues forth."
To emerge when not yet emerged is to emerge in order to proclaim the King of Sutras.

The great Bodhisattvas who surge forth from the earth in the *Lotus Sūtra* enter hundreds of thousands of samādhis within the profound nature of reality (dharmatā) where they had not previously entered; this is called "skillful entry. Their emergence and abiding are likewise so.
If it is thus even for a bodhisattva, it can be known that it is so for the resultant Buddha.

First, the direct explanation according to the text, in two parts:
first, the elucidation of "immeasurable and profound.

Being about to clearly demonstrate the sphere of the Buddha’s entry, one must first distinguish and reveal the loftiness and vastness of its essence; thus, the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is used to manifest its vastness.
The Dharma of the Middle Way takes that which is not a realm (*dhātu*) as its realm; since this realm has no exterior, it is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
Furthermore, its loftiness is revealed through the three truths (*trisatya*).

Although both the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional are equally consummate, they are accessible to the Two Vehicles and realized only partially by Bodhisattvas; if the middle truth were not perfect (*pariniṣpanna*), true wisdom would be unable to realize and enter it.

Now it is clarified that the essence of the three truths is neither superior nor inferior; rather, they are the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), which is the very foundation of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, it is said to "penetrate through to the end," which alone accords with the sutra’s praise of its profound depth.
"Profound" (*shen*) is the meaning of "high.

One must understand that the *dharmadhātu* and the perfect three truths (*triratna*) are non-dual and undifferentiated; here, we take these two names to manifest their immeasurable profundity, making them easier to perceive.
Having first manifested [the meaning], it is next distinguished:
if categorized by the Two Vehicles, the Perfect is distinguished from the Partial;
if categorized by the Bodhisattvas, the Deep is distinguished from the Shallow, for all those below the Buddha are considered lower stages.
Even the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is still simple; how much more so the Three Teachings?
Second, under the character "Dharma" (*fa*), the two characters "dharma-nature" (*faxing*) are explained.
Above, it was clarified that "lofty and vast" constitutes the virtue of the essence (*ti*); now, it is clarified that dharma-nature constitutes the essence of these virtues.
Explaining the meaning of these two characters reveals the nature of its loftiness and vastness.
That which is called "Dharma" (fa) has the sense of a "normative rule"; the Buddhas take it as their model, thereby accomplishing all virtues.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is what is called the Dharma.
Yet, regarding this nature of phenomena (dharmatā), who among those of the three vehicles or the six realms does not rely upon it as a standard for their establishment?
Because they are deluded regarding the inherent nature and its functional manifestations, they act contrary to the norms despite following them; thus, the three obstacles are formed.
It is like the seven assemblies of the Sangha—who among them does not take the Buddha as their teacher?
Because there are both oppositions and conformities, there is consequently the distinction between bondage and liberation.
Now, in order to manifest that which we take as our teacher by means of the ultimate conformity, it is said: "That which serves as the track for all Buddhas is called the Dharma."
What is called "nature" (xing) has the meaning of "unchanging," because the substance of the four virtues does not undergo transition or alteration.

One must know that these four pervade all phenomena; even down to the environment and its inhabitants, the causes and effects within the hells, each and every one is none other than permanence, bliss, self, and purity. This is what is meant by the phrase "the characteristics of the world are eternal."
2. From "It is not this" (*na etad*) onwards, there is a further interpretation based on the meaning, in three parts:
first, an interpretation based on what is illuminated by true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
"The knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*) means that the afflictions have already been completely severed.
The knowledge of non-arising means that delusions will not arise again.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* explains these two knowledges, saying: "In the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), if one correctly knows for oneself:
'I have known suffering, I have abandoned its origin, I have realized its cessation, and I have cultivated the path,' this is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)."

"If one correctly knows for oneself, 'I have already known suffering; there is nothing further to be known,' and explains the subsequent three cases in the same manner, this is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* defines the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) as the exhaustion of afflictions, and the knowledge of non-arising as the non-production of future retribution.

Both of these two wisdoms illuminate the partial emptiness; this briefly distinguishes them from the Two Vehicles, while their intent encompasses the Bodhisattvas up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment.
Because the dharma-nature of the Two Vehicles is not the Middle Way, it is shallow; because it does not fully possess both form and mind, it is limited.

Regarding "knowledge of reality as it is" (*yathābhūtajñāna*), the *Śāstra* clarifies eleven types of knowledge; the first ten are shared with the two vehicles, whereas only the knowledge of reality as it is is not shared.
This refers to the realization, in accordance with reality, of the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena, without any obstruction.
This wisdom illuminates horizontally and penetrates vertically; it is the present *dharmatā*.
2. From "Furthermore, there is also... below, the explanation proceeds by showing that the principle is identical with the phenomena.
The profound and vast *dharmatā* is the dwelling place where the Buddha roams; furthermore, it transcends the pure conduct of the bodhisattvas.

The fear that [the meaning] will not be understood refers to the concern that ordinary, base people might think that, apart from the causes and effects of the primary and secondary aspects of form and mind, there exists a separate dharma-nature where the Buddha dwells; therefore, [the text] specifically negates this. It does not mean that there is a separate dharma called "immeasurable" or "profound."
However, the term "all places" must encompass the three lands (*tridhātu*), and all phenomena should properly correspond to the causes and effects of the nine realms (*navadhātu*).

If the Buddha-dharma of Vairocana were exclusively pure and exclusively good, then the defilements and evils of the three lands and nine realms would have to be severed; how, then, could they be called "all being Buddha-dharma"?

Therefore, one should understand that all defiled and evil states are none other than the intrinsically endowed nature; the Buddha-nature as the conditions and the understanding is not exclusively good and pure, for the defilement of the nature and the evil of the nature are entirely the conditions and the understanding.

If all such phenomena are the Buddha-nature, then the three lands and nine realms—whose cultivated defilements are essentially void—are, in their fundamental nature, the ten realms of inherent virtue; this is the essence of perfect enlightenment, omnipresent and without exception. Only then can it be said that Vairocana pervades all places, and that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma.
What single thought-moment, single particle, or single person is not the *dharmatā* in which the Tathāgata dwells?
Therefore, it is called "immeasurable.

Furthermore, one must understand that all defiled and evil phenomena are profound in their very essence; thus, they are said to be "extremely deep," yet this profundity is not some separate reality existing apart from them.

Therefore, it is said that phenomena are themselves reality, and form and fragrance are the Middle Way. Because of form, fragrance, and so forth, deluded minds claim they are merely partial aspects of form; yet when understood, there is nothing that is not the entirety of the Dharma-realm, because they are simply form, simply sound, simply fragrance, simply taste, and simply touch.
If there were even a speck of dust’s worth of phenomena existing apart from form, it would not be called "only" (yogācāra), nor would it be the Middle Way.
The Middle Way is secret, subtle, and its contemplation is inexhaustible; thus it is termed "profound."
III. Regarding the section beginning with "For example," there are two parts:
first, citing analogous cases;

second, from "In accordance with this" onwards, providing an interpretation based on those cases, which has three sub-sections: 1. Citing analogous cases; 2. [Interpretation based on the analogy]; 3. [Conclusion].
First, the Middle Truth is explained as being immeasurable.

The treatise clarifies the four immeasurables—namely, loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). They are called "immeasurables" (*apramāṇa*) because they are directed toward immeasurable objects; they are called "equalities" (*sama*) because they arise from a mind that is impartial. This refers to those with sentient beings as their object (*sattvālambana*).
Based on the extent of their objects—whether narrow, broad, or vast—they receive three names: namely, "broad," "vast," and "immeasurable.
Now, following that analogy, these three names are established here based on the distinction between the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti).

The Sūtra demonstrates wandering within the immeasurable dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), thereby revealing the principle of the perfect fusion of the Middle Way; it is not merely the reality of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) nor the conventional of partial existence.
Second, from "If [one] conditions... onwards, it clarifies that the Middle Way must necessarily encompass and integrate all things.

The Buddha may, in response to specific capacities, employ provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) to illuminate the two truths (*satya*) exclusively; since this does not encompass the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*), it does not constitute wandering within the immeasurable *dharmatā*.

Now, employing ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) to illuminate the principle of the Middle Truth, there is nothing that the Middle does not encompass; thus it is said that "if one takes the Middle Way as the object, then the three wisdoms are a single mind," and for this reason, the Middle Truth is termed "immeasurable."
3. From "This" onwards, the correspondence between the object and wisdom is concluded.
As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Only the Buddha thoroughly exhausts the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena."
How could the principle of the provisional and the real ever reach its ultimate limit?
It is truly because the Buddha has attained inexhaustible wisdom that he is able to exhaustively investigate it.
Now, it is likewise so.
The wisdom of those of the Two Vehicles and of lower stages is limited; therefore, they cannot fathom the limitlessness of that which has no limit, nor the bottomlessness of that which has no bottom.
Second, "All" and below explains the sphere of action of all Buddhas, in two parts:
first, the Dharma.
Students should know that original enlightenment (benjue) is the locus, while initial enlightenment (shijue) is the Buddha.
Original enlightenment is entirely present within initial enlightenment; it is through initial enlightenment that one finally accords with the original.
If this were not so, how could each be described as immeasurable and profoundly deep?

However, although he had already attained union with reality from the moment he first sat at the site of enlightenment, he now manifests the appearance of such union for the sake of guiding sentient beings, stating that he "traverses the spheres of action of all Buddhas.
Second, the illustration by analogy.
The phrase "the place where it is performed" indicates that it is able to encompass [all things].
Third, the conclusion following "transcendence" has two parts:
first, a direct explanation based on the text; second... [the rest of the text follows].
First, a brief explanation based on the meaning;
second, an extensive explanation by citing texts, in two parts:
first, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

The nine kinds of dhyāna are: first, that of intrinsic nature; second, the universal; third, the difficult; fourth, the universal gateway; fifth, that of the virtuous person; sixth, the universal practice; seventh, the removal of afflictions; eighth, pertaining to this world and other worlds; and ninth, the pure and purified.
The text briefly indicates the first and last of the two dhyānas.

As for the ninth dhyāna, one transitions from the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) into Subtle Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); therefore, it is said that all afflictions—both general and specific, whether manifest (*maula*) or residual (*vāsanā*)—are completely exhausted. From the tenth stage downward, there still remain both manifest and residual afflictions.
In the commentary on the *Avataṃsaka*, the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is not separately established; the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) itself is Equal Enlightenment.

As for the statement that both the pervasive and specific afflictions, along with their residual habits (*vāsanā*), are exhausted: "pervasive" refers to the four abodes of attachment (*catur-vāsana*), and "specific" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).
The pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) are exhausted at the level of the seventh stage of the *śraddhā-bhūmi* (the stage of faith) in the Perfect Teaching;

as for the residual habits (*vāsanā*), they are exhausted upon reaching Buddhahood. This is because our school distinguishes sixteen categories of residual habits within the Small Vehicle by dividing them into four sets of four.

Regarding separate delusions, the stages of severing the forty-two grades are as usual; the details concerning the residual habits (*vāsanā*) are fully explained in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra-vyākhyā*.

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), although all views are severed through the Perfect [Path], residual habits still remain.

The Perfectly Enlightened One enters the Gate of Profound Mystery; having cultivated all matters anew for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, his realization of principle is distinct and clear, yet residual habit-energies remain slight, and phenomena are like a wisp of smoke.
Since he cites the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* regarding the "pure dhyāna purified of all views," he clarifies only the habituation to views (*dṛṣṭi-vāsanā*).

If he were to cite the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* stating that the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) sever the habituation to craving (*tṛṣṇā-vāsanā*), would the ten stages—which are equivalent to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)—not then enter into the profound mystery?

Therefore, it is known that beyond the severance of the primary afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) of the distinct delusions, one further enters the profound mystery to sever the residual habits (*vāsanā*); the text is extremely clear on this point.
Second, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*.

The Buddha’s mind of intrinsic purity transcends all meditative concentrations attained through cultivation; therefore, it is said that "the mind being pure, he has already crossed beyond all dhyānas.
Furthermore, because he has reached the further shore of all meditative concentrations, it is said that he has "already crossed."
2. From "Also, it is" below, the meaning is explained again by restating the intent.
The Buddha does not exalt himself; he is exalted because he relies on the Dharma.
Now, by clarifying the high position, the intention is to distinguish and reveal the loftiness and profundity of the *dharmatā*.
2. From "This is gold" onwards, the specific descriptions are set forth in two parts:
first, it clarifies that the meaning of the description differs from what preceded.
Yet, do not the various chapters previously described all fall within these five meanings?

Since the seventeen chapters discuss only the three dharmas—generally clarifying their specific characteristics and the teachings intended for sentient beings—their names and so forth are not explicitly set forth as they follow from the chapters.

Therefore, I shall now clearly demonstrate that the text of the "Introduction Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) fully enumerates the five meanings, enabling students to know that this single scripture, from beginning to end, explains nothing other than name, essence, tenet, function, and the characteristics of the teaching. Only then will they understand that the commentary on the title exhaustively captures the intent of the entire sutra.
2. From "The first ten" onwards, the meaning is explained based on the text, in two parts:
first, the division of the text;
second, from "The commentator" onwards, the explanation of the meaning, in two parts: 1. Division of the Text. 2. Explanation of the Meaning, in two parts: [from "The commentator" onwards].
First, the exposition of the four meanings, which has four parts.
First, one sentence expounds the name, which has two parts.
First, the interpretation by others that it belongs to the essence (*svabhāva*).
Regarding "ore" (*kōngshí*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "'Kōng' refers to the raw ore of copper and iron.
As for "internal and external use," light constitutes internal use, because it manifests the essence from within.
Luminosity is the external function because it reflects other objects.

This master also understands that the two characters "luminous" (ming) pertain to the function of the thesis, while "gold" is the essential substance; this is because the substance and its function are inseparable.
Although three characters are designated, the intent lies in the essence.
Second, from "Now I clarify" onwards, the names are now definitively set forth.
Designating three while revealing one does not entirely deviate from reason; therefore, it is said that this is "naturally so."
In the division of the text, there is naturally a sequential order of sentences; it is precisely with the Middle Way as the King of Sutras that the essence [of the teaching] is described.
Why, then, must the first sentence describe the essence while simultaneously encompassing the doctrine and its function?

Students should understand that the phrase enumerating the names is based on the preceding text; it explains that the three-character name is not established through metaphor, but is a direct designation for the profound and vast *dharmatā*. This is because as the Buddha was correctly traversing this *dharmatā*, he immediately proclaimed:
"This is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of all sūtras."
If it is not called "dharmatā," what does this single character "is" (shi) refer to?

The wise, having deeply perceived the subtle purport of the sūtra, have therefore established two types of interpretation: the exegesis based on the literal text (*fùwén*) and the exegesis based on the essential nature (*dàngtǐ*).
To corroborate this with the appended text, it first cites these words: "To establish the title at the very outset makes it all the more credible.
Since this specific intention was already set forth in the preceding appended text, there is no need to further elaborate upon it here when explaining the description of the titles.
Second, the phrase "King of Sutras" and those following describe the essence [of the teaching]. This section has two parts:
first, referring back to the previous text to introduce the present one.

The preceding section—that is, the *Xuanwen*—repeatedly clarifies the "king of emperors" (*dìwáng*) by distinguishing the "King of Sutras" through the gates of encompassing phenomena, encompassing teachings, and encompassing stages; now, this section further elucidates the "king" from the perspective of the Middle Way.
2. From "The Three Baskets" (*Tripiṭaka*) onwards, the section on "Distinguishing and Correcting Others" has two parts:
first, clarifying the interpretations of others, which has two sub-sections;
first, the introductory narration.
The intention of the Tripitaka Master is as follows:
the three characters of the sutra’s title are metaphors for the Three Virtues (triguṇa), which are then correspondingly matched to the three sutras.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* elucidates that the Buddha possesses the substance of liberation, thereby directly severing the view of the two vehicles regarding the extinction into ashes.
The *Prajñāpāramitā* discusses emptiness precisely to eliminate the attachments of ordinary beings.
The *Avataṃsaka* suddenly expounds the principle of the Dharmakāya for those at the stages of the ten faiths and the three levels of worthiness; therefore, it is called "the beginning of practice."
The three aforementioned sutras each discuss a single virtue and each addresses a specific capacity.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, however, fully manifests the three virtues; therefore, it can universally address the capacities of beings across all eight stages.
Liberation covers the two stages of the Two Vehicles;
Prajñā covers ordinary beings, with humans and devas collectively designated as one stage;
and the Dharma-body covers the five stages of the Bodhisattva: faith, abiding, practice, direction, and the grounds.
Since there are none who lack the karmic affinity to receive it, this is the meaning of the King of Sutras exercising universal subsumption.
Second, from "This" onwards, the refutation has two parts:
first, clarifying the contradiction with the intent of the teaching.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* primarily discusses the profound and wondrous three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), which are intended for those with the capacity for the Perfect Teaching; how could they be restricted merely to the followers of the Two Vehicles?
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* fully demonstrates the three kinds of *prajñā*; how could these differ from the three virtues?
How much more so when it is said that the audience consists not of those subject to birth and death—how could they be limited to ordinary worldlings?

The three bodies (*trikāya*) in the *Avataṃsaka* are also the three virtues (*triguṇa*), and since they fully discuss the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), how could they pertain only to bodhisattvas at the initial stage of practice?
This interpretation not only limits the scope of those for whom it is intended, but also fails to manifest the perfect nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmatā*).
Second, from "One who acts thus" onwards, the text clarifies the harm to the practitioner.
Regarding this interpretation of Paramārtha, those with discernment know it to be improper;
yet ignorant people claim that those three sūtras are inferior to this scripture, thereby giving rise to slander and incurring transgression—how can one rely upon them?
Second, from "Now it is said" onwards, the present explanation is clarified in three parts:

first, a general demonstration of the right and wrong of the various scriptural kings, in two sections; first, determining right and wrong by means of the Three Truths, in two sections: 1. A general demonstration of the right and wrong of the various scriptural kings.
2. Determining right and wrong by means of the Three Truths. (Regarding the second section: First, determining right and wrong by means of the Three Truths. (In two sections: First...
First, the demonstration of the three truths.

Within the various divisions of the teachings throughout the one lifetime of the Buddha, some take the expressive words and letters as the sūtra; some take the expressed meaning and principle as the sūtra; and some take the union of words and meaning as the sūtra. Therefore, the sūtras of the one lifetime do not go beyond being either a union of words and meaning or their lack thereof.

If they do not accord [with ultimate truth], the texts that express them belong only to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and do not transcend three types: namely, the conventional of substantial existence according to the Tripiṭaka; the conventional of illusory existence according to the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*); and the conventional shared by both the illusory existence and the illusory existence-as-emptiness according to the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*).

If the principle being expounded consists solely of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it likewise comprises only three types: namely, the true [nature] of the extinction of substantial existence in the Tripiṭaka; the true [nature] of illusory existence as identical to emptiness in the Shared Teaching; and the true [nature] of neither existence nor non-emptiness in the Distinct Teaching.

Within these six, three types of ultimate truth do not inherently possess the conventional; rather, one enters the ultimate by means of the three conventionalities. Since the conventional must ultimately be extinguished, the [proposed] definition does not hold.

If the principles and the text are harmonious, they do not exceed three types: namely, the Perfect teaching that connects to the Shared, the Perfect teaching that connects to the Distinct, and the Properly Perfect teaching.
In these three, the essence of both the ultimate and the conventional is the Middle Way.

Why is this? In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the ultimate truth and the conventional truth have always mutually interfused. If one connects with the teachings of the Shared and Distinct Teachings, the ultimate truth they expound is already the "tendency of all dharmas" (*sarvadharma-gati*); even when focusing specifically on the conventional texts, these are likewise the "tendency of all dharmas. Therefore, in these three types of teaching, the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual; this is called the "convergence of principle and text," whereby the meaning of the Middle Way is established.
Because the ultimate is identical to the conventional, the ultimate is not the ultimate;
because the conventional is identical to the ultimate, the conventional is not the conventional.
When neither ultimate nor conventional applies, speech and thought naturally cease; it is only by force of convention that we give it the name "the Middle."
Question:
In the Separate Teaching, conventional reality as a manifold, illusory existence may be considered the expressive text; however, how can emptiness itself also be considered text?
Answer:
"Phrasing" (wen) refers to the characteristics of phrasing; it is that which can express and manifest meaning.
If the meaning pertains to the emptiness of the Shared Teaching, then the principle to be expressed is the forgetting of characteristics.

Now, in the Distinct Teaching, both extremes possess characteristics, yet these serve as the means of manifestation to reveal the "neither-of-the-two. Therefore, both emptiness and existence are considered "phrasing."
Question:

Since all seven categories, beginning with the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), are designated as both ultimate and conventional, how is it that the latter three are designated as the Middle Way?
Answer:
How could one hear that the ultimate and the conventional lack a middle?

For instance, in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), as well as in the teachings that connect with or are distinct from [the Separate Teaching], these three—ultimate, conventional, and middle—are all termed "inconceivable. How, then, could they not be the Middle Way?

As explained in the *Nirvāṇa-śū* regarding the sevenfold two truths (*dvaya-satya*), three among them are also designated by the name "Middle Way" (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Why, then, do you single out this one for criticism?
Question:
If we take its meaning, the *tattva-satya* (True Truth) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*) is neither empty nor existent; why is it not called the "Middle"?
Answer:
To abide in the middle while departing from extremes is inconsistent with the principles of the text.
The initial mind cannot attain it; thought and deliberation must be suddenly forgotten.
If one looks toward the Perfect [Teaching], it is merely the True [Meaning] as expressed by the conventional;

therefore, the preceding passage explains the Sūtra in this way, yet it specifically states regarding the Perfect, "breaking away from and clarifying within the Middle. This is truly because that which is expressed is not identical to the expression itself and thus is not called the Middle Way; only when the nature of words is detached and there is nothing that is not Buddha-dharma is it called the Perfect Teaching—the Middle Way being thus.
Question:
Why is it that only the "separate connection" (biete jietong) is excluded?
Answer:

Now, when the ultimate and conventional truths are contrasted with principle and phenomena, their distinction regarding the "reception of connection" is already included within the six internal categories.
Why is this? If one has not yet received such connection, then illusory existence must be explained as being identical to emptiness.
If, after being received [into the teaching], one belongs to the "Middle Only" (but-madhyamaka), it is limited to illuminating the conventional within the complex [of truths].
Therefore, since the essence of the Dharma is already included within the first six [categories], what remains to be omitted?
Moreover, the present text does not explicitly state that there are seven kinds of two truths; rather, it clarifies the adoption of both text and principle throughout the entire dispensation.

Taking the principles and the patterns together, there are the three types of conventional sutras, the three types of true sutras, and the three types of middle-way sutras; through such clarification of the scriptures, everything gathered within a single transformation is exhaustively encompassed, leaving nothing out.
There are those who establish nine types of sutras based solely on the name *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, taking the individual characters as the fundamental basis for their meaning.
That is to say: if one grasps the three characters as the expressive text (*vyañjana*), they are called the three kinds of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
if one grasps the three characters as the rational essence (*tattva*) expressed by them, they are called the three kinds of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If one grasps the principle that "conformity with the text" means not being biased toward either extreme, it constitutes the threefold Middle Way.
If this is how it is explained, how could it be merely a matter of interpreting the meaning according to one's own subjective mind?
Is this not a stubborn departure from the intended meaning of the text?

To explain the first two instances of the character "take" (*qu*) as "clinging attachment," yet to explain the final instance of "take" as "not being partial or attached"—what kind of statement is this?
The Great Master, as the sovereign who elucidates all sutras, established nine categories to encompass the teachings of his entire life.
Since this sutra expounds the sovereignty of the Middle Way, it attains mastery over these nine categories and is thus named the King of All Sutras.
For what reason do these nine types consist of only three characters?
It is because the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* itself is the sovereign king of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*.
Since it lacks the other sūtras, it would not be a complete universal sovereign.
There are many such contradictions, yet I shall discuss only these two.
Second, from the words "If one says" onwards, the correct and incorrect positions are determined.

If within various schools there are those who claim that the first three [aspects] can express conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), or those who claim that the first three are what express ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and their essential natures do not accord, they are all termed "other truths"; they may obtain this sūtra, but it is not called the "King of Sūtras."
Because it does not clearly comprehend the ultimate truth while possessing the conventional, the conventional truth is not identical to the ultimate truth.
Since both the conventional and the ultimate lack the sense of being a sovereign ruler, they are not "kings."

If within certain schools there are those who say that the three kinds of conventional truth are the ultimate and the ultimate is entirely conventional, and that the non-duality of these two truths is called the Middle Way, such that outside this Middle Way there is not even the slightest phenomenon;

As this sutra states: "the immeasurably profound dharma-nature," and again, "the inconceivable realm of wisdom," and further, "abiding in the suchness of all dharmas, containing all dharmas within all dharmas"—if so, there is nothing that can be expressed (the signified) outside of what expresses it (the signifier), and how could there be anything that is expressed outside of what expresses it?

Since both the principle and the expression are harmonious and the Middle Way is thus perfected, this sutra attains the status of a king; it thereby achieves mastery over the ninefold categories of the three mundane, the three true, and the three middle [teachings].
Question:
Since the essence of the sūtra is already the sovereign among the three types [of scriptures], why does it further state that it is "sovereign over the nine"?
Answer:

The preceding analysis of the nine types was a general overview based on the three conventional, three real, and three middle [truths], demonstrating that within the scriptures of a single lifetime there are both partial and perfect teachings.
Now, in judging the various sections [of the canon], wherever a single passage explains the perfect Middle Way, that scripture is the King of Sutras.
It is able to universally demonstrate nine kinds of mastery; among the three [categories], the sūtras are simply alternative names for these.
Since their essence is identical, they attain mastery.
As for the other six sūtras, they are the skillful means employed within the Perfect Teaching; how could a king not be master over his ministers?
2. From "But the Sūtra" onwards, the section reveals its supreme majesty by means of the Middle Way, in three parts:
First, it clarifies that the perfect essence of all sections constitutes the King.
The essence of the King of Sūtras of the Middle Way is one; however, it establishes various names according to the inclinations and preferences of sentient beings.
Therefore, the preceding text states: "If one speaks of the Middle Way, this is the Sūtra; this is the King.
Which sūtra is being spoken of?
It refers to the *Avataṃsaka* and other sūtras within the four flavors (*catur-rasa*), which establish the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and so forth as the essence of the sūtra.
However, one must distinguish within the four flavors which sutras are the "kings" and which are not.
For example, within the Avataṃsaka section, there are three types of sutras: those in the *Zhengyuan* (Perfectly Round) and the *Jiebie* (Connected Distinct) sections are sutras that are kings;
whereas within the *Zhengbiejiao* (Distinct Teaching of the Correct) section, these sutras are not kings. Therefore, regarding the Dharma-body, it is necessary to make such distinctions.
In the Tripiṭaka, there are only the two truths of emptiness and reality, and these sutras are not "Kings.

Within the Vaipulya division, nine types of sutras are present: those of the Perfectly Complete Teaching (Yuanjiao), those where the Perfect connects to the Distinct (Bie), and those where the Perfect connects to the Shared (Tong). These three are the "Sutra Kings"; therefore, the name "True Mark" (Shixiang) applies to all three of these types.
The remaining six are sūtras and cannot be considered kings.

Within the Prajñāpāramitā section, there are no two belonging to the Tripiṭaka; there are seven types of sūtras, which are likewise equal to the Vaipulya. Three of these are sūtra-kings and are given the name "Mother of the Buddhas" (Buddhamātṛ); the remaining four are not kings.
The *Lotus Sūtra* is the single perfect [teaching]; this sūtra is the king, for by opening up the provisional means, it unties the topknot and bestows the jewel.
The nine kinds of [teachings] in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* are all known to be within the Perfect; none of them fail to be the king of sūtras.
All sentient beings shall surely attain Buddhahood; who, then, would not take the true cause as their teacher?

Therefore, within the great Mahāyāna sūtras, this King of Sutras on the Middle Way exhibits variations in length and brevity, yet it establishes the single *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) under these diverse names as the essence of all sutras.
2. Below the section on "Analogies," the text provides analogies based on the kings of successive generations.
"Various clans" refers to the clans of the Three Augusts and Five Emperors.
Fuxi, the Great Clarifier, was of the Feng clan; Shennong, the Divine Farmer, was of the Jiang clan; and Youxiong, the Yellow Emperor, was of the Gongsun clan—these were the Three Augusts.

Shao Hao, Lord of the Golden Heaven; Zhuanxu, Lord of Gao Yang; and Di Ku, Lord of Gao Xin—these were all of the Ji clan. Di Yao, Lord of Tao Tang, was of the Yi Qi clan; Di Shun, Lord of You Yu, was of the Yao clan. These are the Five Emperors.
Thus it is said that "the various clans" [arose].
Regarding "successively flourishing in response to the cycles," this refers to responding to the cycles of the Five Elements (Wuxing) as they mutually generate one another.
Fuxi responded to the Wood cycle, Shennong to the Fire cycle, and Huangdi to the Earth cycle; the Five Emperors may be inferred in sequence from these.
Regarding the "Dragon Masters" (Long-shi): because Fuxi initially received an auspicious omen of dragons upon his establishment, he recorded the dragon in his official titles.
Thus, the *Zuo Zhuan* states: "The Lord Taihao recorded the dragon; therefore, he appointed Dragon Masters and gave them dragon names."
Regarding the "Office of Birds": when Shao Hao first established his reign, there was the auspicious omen of the phoenix;

therefore, he designated officials by means of birds. Thus, the *Zuo Zhuan* states: "When Shao Hao Zhi ascended the throne, the phoenix arrived; therefore, he appointed bird-masters and gave them names based on birds."
"Those who establish hegemony according to the times" refers to kings who, responding to the destiny of their era, rule over the world.
Although the hundred generations differ—meaning their dynastic titles and eras are distinct—their status as sovereigns is one and the same; they are all lords of the world.
3. Below "Dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena), it is shown that names are established according to their respective sections in accordance with the analogy.
Although names arise and perish, the essence neither increases nor decreases; therefore, from the Dharmakāya down to the Teacher of Buddhas, each attains mastery within the nine kinds of sūtras.
First, the preceding exhortation states: "Though a hundred generations may differ, the sovereign who unifies them is one.
Second, from the phrase "The Dharma-nature as... onwards, the specific nature of this scripture, the King of Sutras, is clearly elucidated.
Since its principles and expressions are harmonious and it takes the Middle Way as its essence, this constitutes a comprehensive explanation.
If one were to categorize the distinct titles of the essential bodies (*śarīra*) of various scriptural divisions, this sutra specifically takes the King of Dharmatā as its scriptural body.
Because the Buddha wanders within the profound and vast *dharmatā*, he immediately proclaims:
"This is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of all sūtras.

Is this not a definitive indication that the *dharmatā* in which he wanders is the very essence (*tattva*) designated by the name *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, and that this essence is itself the sovereign king of all sūtras?
Question:
Since all three types of sūtra-kings may serve as the essence of Mahāyāna sūtras, to which king does the essence of this sūtra belong?
Answer:

Although the literary expression of the Dharma-nature resides in the Perfect [Teaching], it is permitted that those of the Three Vehicles rely upon this for repentance; therefore, the Great Master explained its essence from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching while judging its doctrinal classification as belonging to the Shared [Teaching]. In meaning, this corresponds to the Perfect Teaching entering into the Middle Way of the Shared [Teaching] to serve as the King of Sutras.
Question:

The *Vimalakīrti-mysteries* states: "If the three kinds of conventional truths within the principle are not the essence of this sutra, then the three kinds of ultimate truths—which are the dharma-nature and true reality—are what constitute the essence of the sutra."
Now, it is said: "If one takes the principle and the text and combines them as a sūtra, this constitutes the threefold Middle Way.

Since the principle and the text are already combined, both the ultimate (paramārtha-satya) and the conventional (saṃvṛti-satya) are the middle; thus, the conventional truth may itself constitute the essence of the sūtra.
Is this not in contradiction with that meaning?
Answer: These two are perfectly consistent; there is no contradiction.

This is because the essence of the sūtra has never been separate from its words, yet the words do not reach it; only when one realizes the truth through phenomena is that truly the essence of the sūtra.

If the essence is categorized according to the two truths, it belongs to the Truth of Ultimate Reality; if categorized according to the three truths, the essence resides in the Middle Way. This demonstrates that the essence of the sutra exists precisely at the point where the path of the mind is severed.

If one considers the Tripiṭaka, the Shared, and the Distinct Teachings, even within their respective doctrines it is said that the essence transcends words and thoughts; yet in all these cases, the expressed meaning is not fully possessed by the expression. How, then, could the expression ever coincide with the expressed?
Therefore, while the textual principles of the six types of sutras do not accord with this, they are by no means devoid of reason when compared to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Thus, the Great Master, wishing to reveal the essence of the sutra and demonstrate the gate of transcending conceptual thought, stated: "The textual principle that accords [with reality] is the Middle Way among the three; it is the perfect essence expounded by the teachings of the four flavors."
When discussing principle through its manifestation in texts, the text is itself identical to the principle, and the principle is likewise identical to the text.
Since the text is identical to the principle, the expressive medium is naturally forgotten;
since the principle is identical to the text, the expressed meaning cannot be grasped as a separate entity.
Since subject and object have been severed, the essence of the Middle Way is revealed.
Within that luminous principle, the three kinds of true truths are all perfectly integrated within the Middle; therefore, they are not different from the essence elucidated in the present text.

As cited in the *Myōhon* (Miaoxuan), the *Dilun* quotes Vajragarbha’s explanation of the four propositions—emptiness and existence being non-dual, not different, and inexhaustible—to reveal the essence; though the phrasing differs, the meaning is the same.
The *Shiqian* asks:
"How can emptiness and the provisional serve as the essence of the sūtra?
It answers:

Since it is the inconceivable identity of emptiness and the provisional, it further indicates that emptiness and the provisional are themselves the Middle; thus, the Middle is the essence of the sutra.
Since the Middle is itself emptiness and the provisional, it likewise points back to the Middle.

Those four phrases do not transcend the three truths; because they are perfectly interfused, each of the three truths contains all three. Thus, in these four phrases, every single phrase embodies the three truths; this is why it is said that "the words differ while the meaning remains the same."
Since every phrase possesses the Middle Way, they all constitute the essence.

To investigate and conclude that emptiness and the provisional can serve as the essence is because they possess the Middle; thus it is said: "Returning to point to emptiness and the provisional as being precisely the Middle, the Middle is the essence of the sutra."

Therefore, although the Middle Truth possesses both emptiness and the provisional, emptiness and the provisional are not its essence; thus it is said, "The Middle is emptiness and the provisional," and it also points back to the Middle.
Question:
Why not simply state that the Middle is the essence of the sutra, while emptiness and the provisional are not its essence? This would already suffice for the meaning.

Why is it that after first clarifying that each of the three truths has its own three aspects which can all serve as the essence, one then further selects from within each of these three truths only the "Middle" (emptiness-and-provisionality) to take as the essence of the Sūtra? Is this not redundant and prolix?
Answer:

It is precisely because the meaning of "perfect" (yuan) cannot be established through a singular explanation that this discourse of integration is composed to manifest the wondrous essence. Why is this so?
In essence, emptiness and the provisional are the two aspects of its practice, which constitute the doctrine and function of the sutra;
the Middle Way is the single nature, which constitutes the substance of the sutra.

If one were to claim that only the Middle Way is the substance of the sutra, then the substance would exist separately from the doctrine and function; such a substance would be narrow and incomplete. Therefore, all three truths must be the substance of the sutra.

If one does not select the emptiness and the provisional from each of the three [natures] but takes only the essence of the Middle Way, then one cannot reveal that this essence is neither wisdom nor abandonment.

By discerning the essence in this manner—neither identical to nor separate from the thesis and its function—the realm of conceptual thought is extinguished and purified, and the wondrous essence is spontaneously present.
Since the essence of the Middle Way is thus perfect and subtle, by analogy, the functions of Emptiness and Provisionality are likewise subtle.
Because Emptiness pervades the three truths, this doctrine is not narrow;
because Provisionality pervades the three truths, this function is all the more vast.

Furthermore, one must distinguish between the provisional and the middle within each of the three truths to reveal that the essence is wisdom; likewise, one must distinguish between the empty and the middle within each of the three truths to reveal that the function is cessation. Since these are clarified respectively in relation to the other two as being neither identical nor separate, they are all termed "inconceivable."

If this is so, then not only is its essence the King of Sutras, but its principle and its function are likewise kings; it is thus called the "Three Kings" in summary and distinguished as the "Four Kings" in its teachings, because its single name, single essence, single principle, single function, and single teaching are none other than the Middle Way.
Therefore, the *Xuanyi* states: "The text is titled the 'King of Sutras,' for its teaching encompasses all scriptures.
If even the teaching is called 'king,' then the names [of the other categories] can likewise be understood.

Since every dharma is the Middle Way and none fail to be the essence of the sutra, one must further distinguish and clarify that the name is the means of expression (*abhidhāna*), the thesis is self-realization, the function is the transformation of others, and the teaching is the capacity for discernment; only the essence of the sutra is that which is to be grasped.

Nothing is left uncollected and nothing is omitted in the selection; this accords with all four lines of the *Vajragarbha* [Sūtra]. While the *Shiqian* takes only the middle line from among these four, their underlying intent is merged and unified.

Third, from "If one practices" onwards, the text specifically clarifies that the present exposition accords with principle and benefits sentient beings; it reveals the perfect Middle Way, which transcends all words and thought, as the King of Sutras.
Above, it accords with the Tathāgata’s intent in expounding the essence of reality; below, it responds to the capacity of sentient beings to hear the sutra.

Since we have already discussed the four flavors, all Mahāyāna sutras whose principles and phrasing are harmonious are kings of sutras; how could there be any reason to exclusively exalt our own sutra while disparaging other scriptures?
Compared to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), these two are separated by a gap of ten thousand times ten thousand. III.
From "Subtle and Wondrous" (*miao-miao*) onwards, the exposition of the school's tenets has two parts:
first, the explanation of "subtle and wondrous."
The Tathāgata has thus described the essence of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the King of Sutras; this is the secret treasury expounded by this single scripture.
Those who hear it must contemplate this meaning, and for this reason, it is called "sublime."

If these two characters were mutually deficient as cause and effect, they would not constitute the three dharmas that are eternally present from beginning to end; therefore, by contrasting the ancient [view] with the non-[erroneous], the present correct meaning is revealed.
The cause encompasses the broad ground and the fruit reaches the ultimate wondrous enlightenment; because their stages are divided into six, they are profound and difficult to perceive.

Because all six are identical [to the ultimate], they are neither vertical nor horizontal: they are not vertical because the cause is identical to the fruit, and they are not horizontal because phenomena are identical to principle. The text explains the rational nature and the fruit, and states by way of analogy that "it is likewise so" for the others.
If one understands these six levels of identity (*ji*), the meaning will be entirely consistent.

Second, from "The Four Directions" onwards, the explanation of the protection by the four Buddhas has two parts: first, the explanation according to the teachings (*jiao*). This has two sub-sections: [1] the explanation according to the teachings;
[2] the explanation according to the principle (*li*). (Note: The provided text fragment ends at the first sub-section.)
First, the formal explanation, in two parts:
first, the explanation of the four Buddhas of the four directions.
When the Buddha uttered these words, there was a specific meaning intended to be expressed; this section correctly sets forth the core tenet of the sutra.

The fundamental principle is the fruition-wisdom that darkly accords with the essence of the Dharma-nature; although this essence is one, it opens four gates, namely: wondrous emptiness, wondrous existence, both, and neither.

As clarified in the *Dilun*, the four phrases are used to manifest the essence as the four directions; the resultant wisdom merges with them to constitute the four Buddhas—the intent of this school’s tenet is thus clearly observable.
2. Regarding the section "Explanation" below, there are two parts to the explanation of "upholding.
First, the upholding is explained in terms of the essence and function of the five Buddhas.

Since the central tenet of the present sutra lies in the resultant wisdom of Śākyamuni Buddha, and because one wishes to reveal that this wisdom darkly accords with the principle of the four gates, it is specifically elucidated through the four Buddhas.
This is because the Buddha’s wisdom makes no distinction between self and other, equally merging with the unmoving nature of the Dharma-body; to accord with this nature is called "upholding.

The Dharma-nature is the essence of phenomena, the Buddhas are the wisdom of retribution, and the life-span is its functional application. Since these three are all eternal, they are said to be "immeasurable."
2. From "Faith" (*śraddhā*) onwards, the section explains protection (*rakṣā*) by means of the characteristics of faith and the removal of doubt.
The Buddha protects the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) so that sentient beings do not give rise to inverted delusions.

The characteristic of faith merely traces the eighty minor marks; however, one may be deluded regarding the fundamental permanence of the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*. The four Buddhas reveal this fundamental essence to bring about the realization that the eighty [marks] are themselves the constant function; therefore, it is called "protection."
Second, from "This one" onwards, there is a selection and demonstration.
Referring to the title of the text of this school, this single phrase—though its meanings are manifold—does not transcend three aspects: essence (*tī*), thesis (*zōng*), and function (*yòng*).

Although the preceding section expounds the fundamental principle (zōng), the principle must be darkly unified with the essence (tǐ), and the essence must give rise to function (yòng); therefore, this phrase cannot be explained in isolation.
The four virtues will be discussed later.
Second, from "Contemplation" (*guān*) onwards, it is explained in terms of contemplation.
The preceding exposition of the essence of the sutra concludes that its ultimate meaning resides in the Buddha of the fruit;

when those who are ready for the teaching hear and perceive this, their delusions are shattered and the principle becomes clear. If practitioners of today do not clarify the Buddha within the clarity of their own minds, what benefit is there in merely hearing this teaching?
Therefore, it is commanded that one contemplates the mind to awaken to the Four Truths and the Four Virtues; since these are identical to one's own mind, one avoids "counting the treasures of others.
This passage is divided into two parts:
first, establishing the Perfect Contemplation (yuan guan) in relation to the Truths and the Virtues, which has two sub-sections:
First, regarding the Four Noble Truths, there are two sections.
First, a general clarification of the object and wisdom.

The four gates of the Four Noble Truths encompass both cause and effect; since the gates are opened from the perspective of principle, it is convenient to treat them in terms of the result. However, as for the Truths themselves, because they include Suffering and its Accumulation, they are more appropriate to be correlated with the beginner's mind.

The practitioner should know that the four Buddhas of the four directions symbolize the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths; this is a meditative contemplation formed by entrusting the mind with phenomena through reliance on external objects while simultaneously attaching the characteristics of the Dharma. Therefore, the Four Noble Truths are themselves the single thought-moment of the mind.

The latent mind is suffering (*duḥkha*); manifest delusions are the origin (*samudaya*); immediate wisdom is the path (*mārga*); and primordial quiescence is cessation (*nirodha*). To know these as they truly are is called the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths.
Second, "East" and below, the specific presentation of object and wisdom, in two parts:
first, the observation of the object.

Regarding the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths, previously [the order was] result first and cause last; now, following the sequence from the beginning of the cultivation of contemplation to its final result, mundane and supramundane *samudaya* (origination) and *mārga* (path) are placed before, while *duḥkha* (suffering) and *nirodha* (cessation) follow after.

For those of initial resolve who wish to easily investigate the objects of contemplation, it is appropriate to begin with proximate matters; therefore, following worldly conventions such as the sequence of first and second, the five elements, and the four seasons, the principle of the "four directions" is established so that the Four Truths may be recognized. The primary aim is to establish the contemplation itself, rather than being constrained by formal terminology.
2. From "Contemplating this" onwards, the arising of wisdom is described.

Since one contemplates the Four Truths within a single mind, by contemplating them without ceasing, the eye of wisdom arises spontaneously to maintain and protect [the mind], so that the sublime principle is not lost and inverted delusions do not arise.

However, one must deeply investigate and contemplate that all four truths are termed "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Suffering and its accumulation are contrary to cultivation, yet their essence is inherently evil; thus, what is contrary is itself the compliant. Since the path and cessation require no effort, it is said: "The aggregates and sense bases are all suchness, so there is no suffering to be abandoned;

"Samsara is itself nirvana; there is no extinction to be realized.

Second, from "Furthermore" onwards, [the text] treats it in terms of the four virtues.
Although the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths at the higher level contemplates the single mind, practitioners of all four teachings can cultivate and realize it.
Now, the three contemplations are explained individually according to the four virtues; that which is suddenly cultivated by those at the initial stage belongs to the Perfect Contemplation.
In the East, permanence counters impermanence; when permanence shatters impermanence, the dust and sands are purified. Impermanence counters permanence;

The negation of both counters the two extremes; when the negation of both shatters the two extremes, ignorance and its accumulation become quiescent.

The other three directions are illustrated by this example.

The previously explained enlightened wisdom was merely general illumination; if one does not discuss specific designations regarding the contemplative mind, then contemplating the sutras would not be entirely consistent with the ultimate meaning.

Abstaining from killing corresponds to wood; wood governs growth, and if one kills, there is no growth.

When correlated with the Five Elements, they are already correlated with the Five Stars; the Five Peaks and the Five Repositories simply preside over the Five Elements.

First, the Five Constants.

Zhao Rui’s *Changduan jing* states: "The benevolent person is one who loves. To establish punishments and eliminate harm, while practicing universal love without partiality, is what is called benevolence (*ren*)."
"Yi" (Righteousness) means appropriateness; to clarify right and wrong and establish what may and may not be done is called righteousness.
"Li" (Ritual) means practice; to have measured degrees in advancing and retreating, and distinct divisions between the honorable and the humble, is called ritual.
Wisdom is that which people know; it is called wisdom because it establishes the nature of right and wrong, gain and loss.
Trustworthiness is that which people receive; it is called trustworthiness because it issues commands and decrees to unify the hearts of the people.
Now, refraining from killing is the response to benevolence (*ren*); to kill another is to lack universal love (*jian'ai*).
Refraining from theft is the response to righteousness (*yi*); to steal is what is not appropriate to do.
Refraining from lewdness is the response to ritual propriety (*li*); illicit lust confuses the distinction between the honorable and the humble, thereby violating the measures of ritual.
One should not drink alcohol in the presence of the wise, for when one is intoxicated, one cannot discern right from wrong or gain from loss.
One should not speak falsely in the presence of those who have faith, for if one utters falsehoods, people will not trust or accept one's words.

If one correlates the Five Constant Virtues with the Five Elements, Zheng Kangcheng’s commentary on the "Zhongyong" chapter of the *Liji* states: "The spirit of wood is benevolence; the spirit of metal is righteousness; the spirit of fire is propriety; the spirit of water is trustworthiness; and the spirit of earth is wisdom."

The previous matching of the Five Elements with the Five Precepts was based on this principle; therefore, abstaining from intoxicants is paired with Earth, and abstaining from false speech is paired with Water.
Second, the correspondence with the Five Classics.

The "Non-Killing" [chapter] stands in contrast to the *Book of Documents*. Since the *Book of Documents* begins its account from the reigns of Yao and Shun downward, it honors the system of abdication and regards acts of killing and military conquest with disdain.

The Master, observing that the House of Zhou had become weak and its edicts were no longer enforced, compiled the *Lüshi* (Annals of Lu) to compose the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals) as a substitute for rewards and punishments, so as to strike fear into rebellious ministers and treacherous sons; thus, he cautioned against even the act of stealing.

There are five types of ritual: the *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou), in the duties of the Grand Master of Rites, states: "By means of auspicious rites (*ji-li*), one serves the ghosts, spirits, and deities of the states; 'service' refers to sacrificing, offering, and presenting oblations. By means of calamitous rites (*xiong-li*), one expresses sorrow for the misfortunes of the states; 'sorrow' refers to relieving distress and disasters. By means of guest rites (*bin-li*), one brings the states into close relationship; 'closeness' means causing them to become attached and submissive. By means of military rites (*jun-li*), one unifies the states; 'unification' means intimidating those who are discordant or transgressing the rules. By means of celebratory rites (*jia-li*), one brings the myriad people into close relationship; 'celebration' (*jia*) means goodness."
"It is for this reason that regulations are established based on what the human heart finds good.
Sexual misconduct is intercourse that does not accord with ritual propriety; therefore, auspicious rites (jiālǐ) are employed to serve as a warning against sexual misconduct."
The *Shi* praises the good and satirizes the evil; it is not a work of falsehood.
The *Yi* is a book that exhausts principle and fulfills human nature, a teaching of purity and subtle refinement.

By not killing, the physical form remains complete; by not stealing, painful sensations do not arise; by not engaging in sexual misconduct, perverse thoughts do not emerge; by not lying, the flow of existence becomes pure and substantial; and by not drinking intoxicants, discernment becomes clear and distinct.
Are these aggregates of virtue merely objects? No; they also serve as supports for mindfulness and wisdom. Therefore, one may establish the four foundations of mindfulness within the aggregates:

the foundation of mindfulness on the body within the aggregate of form, the foundation of mindfulness on feelings within the aggregate of sensation, the foundation of mindfulness on phenomena within the two aggregates of perception and mental formations, and the foundation of mindfulness on the mind within the aggregate of consciousness.

First, the four virtues are assigned according to the sūtras.
Those who realize the Mahāyāna understand that the essence of the five precepts is the nature of the mind; whether receiving or upholding them, each act accords with this nature.
The nature is endowed with the four virtues; therefore, the five aggregates are not impermanent, suffering, selfless, or impure—this is the general correspondence.
Furthermore, the five may also be corresponded to the four virtues individually.

Since the mind and the nature of sentient beings are without arising or ceasing, one accords with this nature by upholding the precept against killing; this is wearing the talisman of longevity and immortality, which is the virtue of permanence (*nitya*).

Because the mind and the nature of sentient beings are free from lust and disorder, one accords with this original nature to uphold the precept against sexual misconduct; this is called "entering and exiting without disorder.

Because the mind and sentient beings are, in every thought-moment, true and without falsehood or interval, one accords with this nature to uphold the precept against false speech; this is called "coming and going without interval."
These two correspond to the virtue of purity.

Because the mind and the nature of sentient beings are not clouded or intoxicated, one accords with the fundamental nature by observing the precept against drinking alcohol; this is called "governing the single body," which is the virtue of the self.

The mind and the nature of sentient beings are themselves bodhi; being free from the suffering of greedy seeking, one accords with this original nature by upholding the precept against stealing. This is called establishing the root of the Way, which is the virtue of joy.

Abstaining from false speech engenders trust and compliance; abstaining from theft preserves the resources of others—this is the rule of material support (*sambhāra*).
Since these correspond to the three tracks, they are in profound accord with all threefold dharmas; thus, we know that the five precepts encompass all phenomena without exception.
